extraction.research_question: Not a research paper: a tutorial showing how to use the grf R package for heterogeneous treatment effect (CATE) estimation, doubly robust ATE, best linear projection, TOC/AUTOC evaluation, Qini policy evaluation and interpretable policy learning.
extraction.theory: Robinson (1988) partially linear model and residual-on-residual orthogonality; generalized random forests (Athey, Tibshirani, Wager 2019) using forest weights as adaptive neighborhoods; AIPW/doubly robust scores (Robins, Rotnitzky, Zhao 1994); orthogonal estimating equations and pseudo-outcomes; honesty and subsampling for pointwise asymptotics (Wager and Athey 2018). Section pp.1-6.
extraction.identification: Unconfoundedness given covariates X is assumed, described as a domain-knowledge choice (p.2). Both applied examples use randomized treatment with known propensity W.hat = 0.5 (pp.6-7, 10-11). Missing covariates are assumed missing at random and handled by MIA splitting (p.6).
extraction.data: Example 1: Bruhn et al. (2016) Brazil school-level randomized financial education program; about 17,000 students at 850 high schools; outcome post-treatment financial literacy score; 13 pre-treatment covariates (4-10 percent missing); clustering by school (pp.6-9). Example 2: Carvalho et al. (2016) payday experiment on low-income individuals tested before versus after payday; about 2,500 individuals and 24 pre-treatment covariates; outcome number of correct answers (variable outcome.correct.ans.per.second); 60/40 train/test split and top 10 covariates by variable importance (pp.10-12).
extraction.method: causal_forest with W.hat and clusters; average_treatment_effect (AIPW); best_linear_projection with HC3 cluster-robust SEs; out-of-bag CATE predictions; rank_average_treatment_effect for TOC/AUTOC; variable_importance; double_robust_scores and policy_tree depth-1 for interpretable policies; regression_forest for nuisance Y.hat; maq sister package for Qini and budget policies (described, not run). Tutorial only, no new estimator.
extraction.scope: Software vignette for the grf R package, 2026. Examples concern Brazilian high school students (RCT data from 2016 study) and low-income individuals in the Carvalho et al. payday sample. Generalization beyond these samples is not argued.
key_findings: Financial education program ATE = 4.35 points (SE 0.52), about 0.3 SD of outcome (p.7); the text calls this roughly a quarter SD.
Best linear projection on financial.autonomy.index: coefficient -0.0329 (SE 0.0128, p = 0.0099); students with higher autonomy benefit less (p.7).
Other BLP terms: is.female -0.7268 (SE 0.5307, p = 0.17); family.receives.cash.transfer -1.1992 (SE 0.6526, p = 0.066); is.unemployed 0.3206 (SE 0.6277, p = 0.61) (p.7).
Whole-sample AUTOC using out-of-bag predictions: one-sided p = 0.65, so no reliable heterogeneity signal overall; authors call the evidence suggestive only (p.8).
TOC prioritizing low financial autonomy: AUTOC estimate 0.69, SE 0.22, t about 3.2; bottom 20 percent by autonomy have ATE about 1.1 points above average with CI excluding zero (p.9).
Depth-1 policy tree: assign training if financial.autonomy.index is 41 or below (p.10). Double robust mean scores: control 58, treated 62 (p.9).
Poverty experiment: CATE TOC AUTOC estimate 0.0061 (SE 0.0092), t = 0.67; no evidence of heterogeneity in the held-out test sample (p.11).
Poverty example histogram: most individuals have effects near the overall ATE with some variation (p.8).
The original Carvalho et al. study found no statistically significant average effect; the tutorial cites Farbmacher et al. (2021) for subgroup concerns (p.10).
extraction.limitations: Authors state the out-of-bag TOC test is a pragmatic heuristic without finite-sample guarantees, because the same data build and evaluate the CATE (p.8). Policy tree example is in-sample and the text says a held-out test set would be needed in practice (p.10). Poverty example is moderate in size relative to predictors and possibly underpowered (p.10). Missing data assumed missing at random (p.6). Identification rests on unconfoundedness, a modeling choice (p.2). Cited Wager (2024) book is in preparation.
extraction.measures: Outcomes: financial proficiency score (ATE and SD units, financial literacy); number of correct answers per second in the attention test. Heterogeneity: CATE predictions, AUTOC/RATE (estimate, SE, t), BLP coefficients, variable importance, policy value (double robust mean scores).

summary_md: A 2026 tutorial vignette for the grf R package (Sverdrup, Hadad, Athey, Tibshirani, Wager), not a research paper. It walks through causal forests for conditional average treatment effects, AIPW doubly robust average effects, best linear projection (BLP) of effect heterogeneity on covariates, rank-weighted average treatment effect (RATE) via TOC/AUTOC curves to test whether a prioritization rule actually concentrates the treatment effect, Qini curves for budgeted targeting, and depth-limited policy trees learned from doubly robust scores. Two randomized examples: a Brazilian school financial-education RCT (about 17,000 students, 850 schools; ATE 4.35 points, SE 0.52; whole-sample AUTOC p = 0.65, but prioritizing low financial autonomy gives AUTOC 0.69, SE 0.22) and a payday experiment (about 2,500 people; held-out AUTOC 0.0061, SE 0.0092, no heterogeneity). The authors flag that out-of-bag TOC tests are heuristics without finite-sample guarantees and that policy trees need held-out evaluation. For Paul's systems the value is methodological. Every targeting score he ships (Terrier untapped potential, the Melange PERS persuadability table, receptivity seed_prob) is a hand-built or correlational ranking of who is most movable. grf supplies the standard test of whether such a ranking sorts people by treatment effect rather than by outcome level. None of it transfers without logged treatment assignment (randomized or known-propensity canvass contacts, outreach or money) and outcomes, which none of the systems currently record. Observational use assumes unconfoundedness. Any analysis built on this stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it.

bearings.paper_claim: RATE/TOC tests whether a ranking sorts units by treatment effect. In the Brazil RCT (n about 17,000 students, 850 schools), ranking by low financial autonomy gave AUTOC 0.69 (SE 0.22, t about 3.2). Ranking by out-of-bag forest CATE gave one-sided p = 0.65 (the text says this rejects, which the printed p-value does not). Qini curves for budgeted targeting and depth-1 policy trees from doubly robust scores are described (pp.7-10).

The score is a fixed formula with no effect-heterogeneity estimate and no RATE or Qini check.

extraction.research_question: How can clustered and panel sandwich covariances be provided as one object-oriented R implementation that works for any model with estfun() and bread() methods, and how well do these covariances perform in finite samples beyond lm() and glm()?
extraction.theory: Quasi-maximum likelihood / M-estimation with misspecified likelihood (White 1994); sandwich covariance B M B with bread and meat; cluster-robust meat with G approaching infinity (Cameron and Miller 2015); independence working model of GEE (Liang and Zeger 1986).
extraction.data: Sec 5.1: InstInnovation data from the sandwich package, following Aghion, Van Reenen and Zingales (2013): 803 firms, firm-level panel 1991-1999, citation-weighted patent counts; clustered by company (803 clusters) and by industry. Sec 5.2: PetersenCL simulated benchmark data from Petersen (2009): 500 firms over 10 years, linear model y on x. Sec 6 and Appendix A: Monte Carlo simulations with balanced clusters of 5 observations (up to 50 in Appendix A), G from 10 to 250 clusters, 100 clusters in the main Experiments I-III, cluster correlation rho from 0 to 0.9 via a Gaussian copula, regressor correlation rho_x = 0.25; unit of analysis is the observation within cluster; period is cross-sectional simulation (no calendar period).
extraction.method: Object-oriented sandwich estimators in R package sandwich: vcovCL (one-way and multi-way clustered covariances with HC0-HC3 bias corrections, cluster factor G/(G-1), multi-way inclusion-exclusion sum with odd/even signs, optional multi0 variant), vcovPL (panel Newey-West and Driscoll-Kraay with Bartlett or other kernels, lag NW1987 or NW1994), vcovPC (Beck and Katz panel-corrected SEs, balanced and unbalanced via pairwise or casewise), vcovBS (clustered bootstrap with xy, residual, wild, Mammen, Webb, norm types, R default 250). Benchmarks against lmtest, multiwayvcov, plm, geepack, pcse and lme4 random-intercept models, and GEE with exchangeable correlation.
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. Inference is via Wald tests and 95 percent confidence intervals using the estimated covariance; the paper notes that clustering in treatment assignment matters more than clustering in sampling (Abadie, Athey, Imbens and Wooldridge 2023) when fixed cluster effects are included.
extraction.measures: Standard errors from the candidate covariance matrices; empirical coverage of nominal 95 percent Wald confidence intervals over 10,000 replications (1,000 for bootstrap in Experiment III); HC bias-correction factors HC0-HC3; Driscoll-Kraay and PCSE sandwich forms; comparison of standard errors across methods on real and benchmark data.
extraction.scope: Population: regression models with estfun() and bread() methods (lm, glm, mlm, nls, betareg, clm, coxph, survreg, crch, hurdle, zeroinfl, mlogit, polr, rlm); simulated cross-section and panel data; benchmark data from finance and political-economy style applications. Software era: sandwich 2.4.0 onward, paper computations with sandwich 3.1-3 and R 4.6.1. Not an institutional or historical study.
key_findings: Sec 5.1 (p.17): hurdle negbin on Aghion et al. data with CL clustering by company (803 clusters): institutions in zero part 0.00658, clustered SE 0.00209, p = 0.0016; in count part 0.00397, SE 0.00430, p = 0.357. Only the zero-part coefficient is significant.

Sec 5.1 (p.17-18): usual standard errors greatly overstate precision. Standard and basic sandwich SEs for zero institutions are both about 0.00135 versus 0.00209 under clustering; clustered SEs are about 1.5 to 2 times the basic sandwich SEs.
Sec 5.1 (p.18): the clustered bootstrap (vcovBS, R = 250) agrees closely with CL-1, e.g. count institutions 0.00411 versus 0.00430, at much higher computational cost.

Sec 5.2 (p.18-19): on the Petersen benchmark (500 firms, 10 years), one-way firm-clustered slope SE 0.050596 from vcovCL matches multiwayvcov; plm and geepack give 0.050540 with HC0 and no cluster adjustment.
Sec 5.2 (p.20): two-way firm and year clustering gives intercept SE 0.065066 and slope SE 0.053561 (multi0 = TRUE); the authors caution that year has only 10 clusters, below what theory requires.

Sec 5.2 (p.20-21): Driscoll-Kraay vcovPL with adjust = FALSE gives slope SE 0.028163, identical to plm vcovSCC; PCSE slope SE 0.025276 agrees with pcse, including unbalanced panels (pairwise 0.025338, casewise 0.025241).

Sec 6.2 Experiment I (p.24): with G = 100 clusters of 5 observations and cluster correlation rho up to 0.9, standard, basic, PL and PC covariances lose coverage for the correlated and clustered regressors; CL-0 stays near the nominal 0.95. PL also fails for the uncorrelated regressor x3.

Sec 6.2 Experiment II (p.25): binomial (logit) and Poisson GLMs give results similar to the Gaussian case, so clustered covariances work well with GLMs; random-intercept mixed models differ because they are conditional rather than marginal in nonlinear models.

Sec 6.2 Experiment III (p.26-27): beta, zero-truncated Poisson and zero-inflated Poisson: CL-0 performs well and is similar to bootstrap (R = 250); coverage for zerotrunc and zeroinfl sits slightly below 0.95 regardless of rho, which the authors attribute to the normal approximation rather than to clustering.

Sec 6.2 Experiment IV (p.27-28): at rho = 0.25 and G = 10, standard errors are underestimated in most cases; about 50 to 100 clusters suffice for CL-0. For small G the ordering is HC3 best, then HC2, HC1, HC0; bootstrap is somewhat better than HC0 and HC1 at small G.
Sec 6.2 Experiment IV (p.28): the authors do not find HC3 overly aggressive for small G, contrary to Pustejovsky and Tipton (2018), though HC3 slightly over-corrects for binomial models at G = 10.

Appendix A (p.35-36): with 5 to 50 observations per cluster, PL and PC approach 0.95 only under AR(1) correlation; under exchangeable correlation with correlated or clustered regressors their coverage falls as clusters get longer. Clustered HC0 performs satisfactorily throughout.
limitations: HC2 and HC3 cluster corrections need blocks of the full hat matrix, which no object-oriented extractor provides, so they are available only for lm and glm (Sec 4.1, p.9 and p.13).
Panel estimators PL and PC are unreliable for short panels and with non-decaying autocorrelation (Sec 7, p.28; Appendix A).
Small numbers of clusters bias standard errors downward (G = 10 in Exp IV); the year dimension in the Petersen example has only 10 clusters, so its two-way results are cautioned (p.20).
Residual cluster bootstrap is not well defined for unbalanced clusters and only issues a warning (p.16).

The fixed-G asymptotic framework is not pursued (p.4). Main simulations use balanced clusters of size 5 and at most three regressors with fixed coefficient vectors, fixed beta precision 10 and zero-inflation probability 0.3.
The authors explain the below-0.95 coverage for zero-truncated and zero-inflated Poisson by the normal approximation but do not test this explanation (p.26-27).
The xy bootstrap makes the same assumptions as the asymptotic estimator, so its results converge to it and may be unnecessary when the asymptotic estimator is available (p.15).
Multi-way clustering default follows Ma (2014) and differs from multiwayvcov unless multi0 is set (p.13, p.20).
Clustered estimators are unavailable when a model package lacks estfun() (p.15).

summary_md: Zeileis, Koell and Graham (JSS 95(1), 2020; reprint run on sandwich 3.1-3) describe the sandwich package's object-oriented clustered and panel covariances: vcovCL (one-way and multi-way, HC0-HC3, G/(G-1) adjustment, odd/even inclusion-exclusion with an optional multi0 swap), vcovPL (panel Newey-West and Driscoll-Kraay), vcovPC (Beck-Katz PCSE) and vcovBS (clustered bootstrap). Worked examples reproduce multiwayvcov, plm and pcse to six decimals on the Petersen benchmark. On the Aghion et al. hurdle model, clustered SEs come out roughly 1.5 to 2 times the basic sandwich SEs. The Monte Carlo (10,000 replications, clusters of 5) finds CL-0 coverage near 0.95 across lm, GLMs, beta and count models once G is around 50 to 100. At G = 10, standard errors are underestimated, and the order from best to worst is HC3, HC2, HC1, HC0. The bootstrap is only somewhat better than HC0 and HC1 at that size. Panel NW and PCSE fail when panels are short or the dependence is exchangeable rather than decaying. The main relevance to Paul's systems is the Mentat sector growth study. Its two-way sector-by-year CR1 sensitivity in sgs_review.R is Equation 20 of this paper, implemented by hand. Its primary inference clusters by 5 to 9 sectors. That is below the paper's smallest tested G of 10, a size the paper already shows to be anti-conservative for CR1-type errors. The study's choice of a wild cluster restricted bootstrap with Webb weights, rather than CR1 t-tests, is therefore the right instinct. However, this paper does not test WCR bootstrap-t (its vcovBS is a variance bootstrap), so it neither validates nor refutes that choice. The SEATS-W test treats Newey-West HAC as secondary with no p-value, which matches the paper's finding that panel NW is unreliable. The paper has no bearing on networks, lobbying identity or allocation.

extraction.research_question: How can sandwich (robust) covariance matrix estimators be computed in general parametric models fitted by estimating functions, not only in lm(), so that inference such as partial z or t tests is robust to some model misspecification.
extraction.theory: M-estimation and estimating-function theory (White 1994; Stefanski and Boos 2002). Sandwich form S = B M B with B the inverse expected negative derivative of the estimating function and M the variance of the estimating function (Eq. 4-6, p.2-3). For models where the objective depends on x and theta only through the linear predictor, the estimating function is r(y, eta) times x (Eq. 7-8, p.4), which justifies HC-type meat estimators. Consistency of theta-hat still requires correctly specified estimating functions (p.3, p.13).
extraction.data: No empirical sample in the theory sections. Illustration 1 (Sec 5.1, p.9-11): simulated count data, n = 250, one regressor x ~ N(0,1), y negative binomial with log-mean 1 + x and size 1, seed 123, R 3.5.0 RNG. Illustration 2 (Sec 5.2, p.11-13): Fair's affairs data from the AER package, n = 601 individuals, response number of affairs (tobit) and binary affairs > 0 (probit); covariates age, yearsmarried, religiousness, occupation, rating. Benchmarks are Greene (2003) Table 22.3 values.
extraction.method: Object-oriented R infrastructure in the sandwich package: generics bread() (default Hessian-based bread, Eq. 9, p.5), estfun() (n x k matrix of empirical estimating functions, p.6), meat() outer-product estimator (Eq. 10, with optional n/(n-k) adjustment, p.6), meatHAC() with weights over lags (Eq. 11, p.7), meatHC() with diagonal omega(r, hat, df) (Eq. 12, p.8), and sandwich() = (1/n) B M B (p.8-9). Wrappers vcovHAC(), vcovHC(), kernHAC(), NeweyWest(), weave(). Inference via lmtest coeftest() and waldtest(), car linear.hypothesis(). Methods are demonstrated for glm (poisson, quasipoisson, glm.nb), survreg via tobit(), and glm probit.
extraction.identification: Robustness comes from the sandwich variance, not from a new estimator. Validity needs consistency of theta-hat under the assumed estimating function (p.3, p.13). HC extension beyond HC0/HC1 additionally needs a linear-predictor structure, a model.matrix method, and hatvalues method for HC2-HC4 (p.8). No formal asymptotic theorem is proven in this paper; it refers to White (1994) Theorem 6.10 and Lumley and Heagerty (1999).
extraction.scope: Parametric regression models fitted by estimating functions in R: linear models, GLMs (Poisson, negative binomial, quasi-Poisson, probit), nls, survreg (tobit via AER), coxph, rlm. Cross-section (HC) and time-series (HAC) settings. Era: 2006 software paper; R 2.x-era package sandwich. Not an inference package itself.
key_findings: Sandwich form S = B M B with M = VAR[psi] and B = inverse expected Hessian (Eq. 4-6, p.2-3); estimator is S-hat = (1/n) B-hat M-hat B-hat (p.8-9).
Poisson fit on overdispersed NB data: naive z-test of I(x^2) is -2.12, p = 0.034; sandwich SE 0.0363 gives z = -1.35, p = 0.18 (Sec 5.1, p.10-11).
Quasi-Poisson gives the same conclusion: I(x^2) SE 0.0506, z = -0.97, p = 0.33; glm.nb gives coefficient -0.0527, SE 0.0649, z = -0.81, p = 0.42 (p.11).
Poisson coefficients track the true conditional mean (intercept 1.0633, x 0.9961, true values 1 and 1); only dispersion is misspecified (p.10).

Tobit on Fair's affairs (n = 601): HC SEs only slightly differ from model SEs; religiousness SE 0.4038 vs sandwich 0.3999; rating -2.2850 with SE 0.4078 vs sandwich 0.3935; age SE 0.0791 vs sandwich 0.0889 (p.12).
Tobit: age p-value moves from 0.0234 to 0.0437 with sandwich, still significant at 5 percent; occupation remains insignificant (0.200 vs 0.185) (p.11-12).
Probit on Fair's affairs: age z = -2.13, p = 0.0328 (model) becomes z = -1.95, p = 0.0508 (sandwich), a change in significance at 5 percent; rating z = -5.19 to -5.12 (p.12-13).
Author's caveat: sandwich errors lose power when the model is correctly specified, and are useful only if the estimates remain consistent, i.e. misspecification causes no bias (p.14).
The paper claims the same qualitative interpretations for tobit and probit under HC and model-based SEs, so HC is not a power-free default (p.12-13).
extraction.limitations: Author states the sandwich package contains no inference functions (p.14). Consistency under misspecification is only partly understood outside linear models (p.14). HC2-HC4 and HAC weights are described only by reference to Zeileis (2004) and Andrews (1991) (p.7-8). Examples use one simulated dataset and one real dataset; no simulation coverage, no coverage-rate study. Finite-sample n/(n-k) adjustment has no theoretical support for non-linear models (p.6). Restriction testing via sandwich is one of several strategies; Godfrey (2006) and Kiefer and Vogelsang (2002) are mentioned as alternatives (p.14).
extraction.measures: Covariance matrices S-hat, bread B-hat from Hessian, meat M-hat as outer product, HAC weighted autocorrelation sums, HC diagonal weight omega. Test statistics: z for coefficients (coeftest), Wald tests. Outputs: estimates, standard errors, z values, p-values per coefficient (Tables p.10-13).

summary_md: Zeileis (JSS 16(9), 2006; read as the sandwich package vignette) recasts heteroskedasticity-consistent (HC) and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) covariance estimation as a modular sandwich S = (1/n) B M B, where the bread B is the inverse Hessian and the meat M is the variance of the empirical estimating functions. R generics bread(), estfun(), meat(), meatHC() and meatHAC() let one computation serve lm, glm, survreg and other models. Two illustrations show what the correction does. In a Poisson fit to simulated negative-binomial data (n = 250), the naive z for I(x^2) is -2.12 (p = .034); with the sandwich it is -1.35 (p = .18). In a probit on Fair's affairs data (n = 601), age moves from p = .033 to p = .051. The author's own caveat carries the most weight: sandwich errors help only if the point estimates stay consistent, they cost power when the model is right, and the package does no inference itself. For Paul's systems the paper is a method source, not evidence. The Mentat sector-growth study hand-codes the same estimators in base R: HC1 (meat as an outer product with the n/(n-k) factor) as a reference-only error, CR1 and two-way cluster errors, and, in SEATS-W, a Bartlett-weighted Newey-West HAC at 2, 4 and 8 week lags kept secondary with no p-value. The way the system is built already follows the paper's caveat, since primary inference comes from wild-cluster and block bootstraps. The paper's HC meat also ignores cluster dependence, which the study handles separately with CR1. One real gap: HC1 and CR1 are cross-checked against statsmodels in a test, but no comparable second-path check was found for the hand-coded HAC (for example against sandwich::NeweyWest), so under DE-062 those HAC numbers stay UNVERIFIED.

extraction.research_question: How to turn HC (heteroskedasticity-consistent) and HAC (heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent) covariance estimators from the econometrics literature into reusable, modular computational tools in R that plug into fitted models and inference procedures.
extraction.theory: Sandwich form Psi = (X'X)^-1 X'Omega X (X'X)^-1 for OLS (eq. 4-5, p.3-4). HC: plug diagonal Omega estimate with weights omega_i from residuals and hat-matrix diagonal (const, HC0-HC4, p.4-5). HAC: plug estimate of Phi from weighted lagged products of estimating functions V_i (eq. 6, p.6), extending to estimating functions beyond OLS (ML, GMM, QML; footnote 1, p.5). Cites White 1980, MacKinnon and White 1985, Newey and West 1987, 1994, Andrews 1991, Andrews and Monahan 1992, Lumley and Heagerty 1999.
extraction.data: Three illustrative real-world datasets, no new data collected. (1) PublicSchools (Greene 1993 Table 14.1): per capita school expenditure vs per capita income for 51 US states in 1979; after dropping Wisconsin NA the analysed N is 50 (p.10). Unit: US state, cross-section. (2) Investment (Greene 1993 Table 15.1): real investment on real GNP and real interest, time series; period not stated in text (fitted series starts 1964 per appendix code, p.19). (3) RealInt (strucchange package): quarterly US ex-post real interest rate 1961(1)-1986(3), so 103 quarterly observations by calendar count, regressed on a mean (p.13).
extraction.method: Estimator functions in R package sandwich: vcovHC(lmobj, omega, type = HC3 default) for HC; vcovHAC(lmobj, weights, prewhite, adjust, sandwich, order.by, ar.method, data) for HAC. Weight helpers: NeweyWest (Bartlett with lag L, default data-driven bwNeweyWest), weightsAndrews and bwAndrews via kernHAC (default quadratic spectral kernel, VAR(1) prewhitening, AR(1) bandwidth), weightsLumley via weave (truncate C=4 or smooth C=1). Inference: coeftest from lmtest with z tests (df = Inf) or t tests; gefp and sctest for OLS-based CUSUM with kernHAC; Fstats for supF; breakpoints (Bai and Perron 2003 dynamic programming, BIC-chosen partition) with confint using vcov = kernHAC.
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. Consistency of the covariance estimators is asserted from the cited asymptotic theory under regularity conditions (p.3-4, p.6), with no new identification argument. Paper is a software and methods exposition.
extraction.scope: Scope is the general linear model estimated by OLS (lm), with HAC also available for glm and robust rlm (MASS) per p.2-3, and extensions to other estimating-function models per footnote 1 and footnote 2. Era: literature of roughly the last 20 years as of about 2004, software in R 4.6.1 with sandwich 3.1-3, lmtest 0.9-40, strucchange 1.5-4, zoo 1.9-0 (appendix, p.18). Population: applied econometricians using R. Institution: none stated.
extraction.measures: Covariance matrices Psi (HC/HAC sandwich), standard errors (square root of diagonal), z and t statistics, p-values, CUSUM and supF statistics, breakpoint confidence intervals (2.5 and 97.5 percent). HC leverage: hat-matrix diagonal h_i, with delta_i = min(4, h_i/mean h) for HC4.
key_findings: Public schools (Sec 4.1, p.10-11): HC0 gives the quadratic income term I(Income^2) coefficient 1587, SE 830, z 1.91, p 0.056 (weakly significant); HC4 gives SE 5489, z 0.29, p 0.77 (clearly non-significant).
The HC0 vs HC4 difference is attributed to a single high-leverage outlier, Alaska (Figure 2, p.11), with HC4 correcting for leverage.

Investment (Sec 4.2, p.11-13): RealGNP coefficient 0.1691 is significant under all three HAC variants: SE 0.0168 (Newey-West lag 4, no prewhitening, p<2e-16), SE 0.0236 (Newey-West automatic bandwidth with prewhitening, p 7.4e-13), SE 0.0208 (Parzen kernel, VAR(2) prewhitening, no finite-sample adjustment, p 4.7e-16).
RealInt coefficient -1.0014 is not significant under any of the three HAC variants: SE 3.3424, 3.6399, 3.9475 with p 0.76, 0.78, 0.80 respectively (p.12-13).

Intercept under the three HAC variants: SE 18.9583, 24.3742, 24.6639 (p 0.51, 0.61, 0.61) (p.11-13). Paper states the three estimators give slightly different standard errors but agree on the substantive conclusions.

Real interest CUSUM (Sec 4.3, p.13-14): OLS-based CUSUM with quadratic spectral kernel HAC variance (VAR(1) prewhitened, AR(1) bandwidth) crosses its 5 percent boundary; sctest p = 0.0082, indicating a significant change in mean with a clear peak in the early 1980s.

Bai-Perron dating (BIC-minimal partition, 3 segments, two breaks; p.14-15): break 1 at observation 47 (1972(3)) with 95 percent CI 37 to 48 (1970(1) to 1972(4)); break 2 at observation 79 (1980(3)) with 95 percent CI 77 to 81 (1980(1) to 1981(1)).
Footnote 6 (p.15): choosing breakpoints by sequential tests instead of BIC yields an additional breakpoint with rather wide confidence intervals.

Section 3.1 (p.5): paper cites Long and Ervin (2000) concluding HC3 performs best in small samples as it down-weights influential observations; Cribari-Neto (2004) proposed HC4 for influential observations.

Section 3.2 (p.6-8): all implemented HAC estimators are weighted sums of lagged products of estimating functions (eq. 6); kernel weights per Andrews 1991 (Figure 1, p.7) with bandwidth selection by AR(1) or ARMA(1,1) approximation or Newey-West 1994.
limitations: Paper is a software exposition and reports no simulation or Monte Carlo evidence on finite-sample coverage; small-sample performance claims are cited from Long and Ervin (2000) and Cribari-Neto (2004).
Choice of HAC weights and bandwidth (lag L, kernel, prewhitening order, bandwidth selector) changes standard errors and the paper notes results depend on these choices (p.8-13).
HC0 vs HC4 conclusions on the public-schools quadratic term hinge on one outlier (Alaska), as the paper itself notes (p.11).
HAC requires that observations be ordered (order.by, default current order, suited to time series); prewhitening uses VAR(p) with OLS by default (p.6-7).
Weights vectors shorter than n are padded with zeros (footnote 3, p.7), a convention the user must keep in mind.
The breakpoint CI approach needs a function-valued vcov because it is applied to several segments; the sequential-test alternative gives wide intervals (footnote 6, p.15).

summary_md: Zeileis (JSS 11(10), 2004; reprinted as the sandwich package introduction) is a software paper, not an empirical study. It casts HC and HAC covariance estimators as one sandwich form, (X'X)^-1 X'Omega X (X'X)^-1, and gives R tools that plug into coeftest and structural-change tests: vcovHC (const, HC0-HC4, HC3 default) and vcovHAC with Newey-West, Andrews kernel and Lumley weights, optional VAR prewhitening and automatic bandwidth. Three worked examples carry the numbers. On 50 US states (1979 school spending), the quadratic income term goes from SE 830 (HC0, p .056) to SE 5489 (HC4, p .77) because one high-leverage state, Alaska, drives it. On the Greene investment series, three HAC settings move the RealGNP SE from 0.0168 to 0.0236 (about 40 percent) without changing the conclusion. On quarterly US real interest 1961-1986 (103 quarters), a HAC-scaled CUSUM rejects stability (p .0082) and Bai-Perron dating finds breaks in 1972(3) and 1980(3). There is no simulation evidence. Claims about small-sample performance come from Long and Ervin (2000) and Cribari-Neto (2004). For Paul's systems this is a method source for the robust-variance rows in Mentat. The forecast refit calls sandwich::vcovHC HC1 and vcovCL directly. The SEATS-W weekly test hand-codes a Bartlett Newey-West SE at fixed lags 2, 4 and 8 weeks and labels it secondary. The paper's own examples support that design: HAC lag and prewhitening choices visibly move SEs. Its leverage example qualifies the HC1 rows in small refit regressions (df about 11). Nothing here touches the network, lobbying or influence components.

extraction.research_question: How can an agent learn by trial-and-error interaction with an environment to maximize cumulative reward, and what are the key ideas and algorithms for doing so (stated aim: a clear and simple account of the key ideas and algorithms of reinforcement learning, per the Preface to the Second Edition)?
extraction.theory: Markov decision process framework with Bellman equations for value functions (Chapters 3-4); temporal-difference learning (Chapter 6); eligibility traces (Chapter 12); policy gradient methods (Chapter 13); links to animal psychology and neuroscience reward prediction error hypotheses (Chapters 14-15).
extraction.data: No empirical dataset. Simulated 10-armed bandit testbed (2000 randomly generated bandit problems, 1000 time steps each, averaged over 2000 runs) and simulated random-walk and gridworld tasks. Chapter 16 case studies report results from prior work, mainly games (backgammon, checkers, Go, Jeopardy! wagering) and computer systems (memory controller, video games).
extraction.method: Expository textbook with worked examples, pseudocode, exercises and mathematical derivations (optional material in shaded boxes). Simulation experiments compare algorithms, for example greedy versus epsilon-greedy action-value methods on the 10-armed testbed.
extraction.measures: Average reward per step on the 10-armed testbed; RMS error on the random-walk prediction task (Chapter 6); win outcomes and Elo ratings in Go; percentage speed improvement in the memory controller study; estimated probability of winning in TD-Gammon.
extraction.scope: Single-agent sequential decision problems modeled as Markov decision processes or bandits, mainly tabular methods first and then function approximation. Field is artificial intelligence and machine learning, not social science. Relevance to lobbying, elections, persuasion, turnout, networks or text measurement: none of these topics appears in the text. Closest overlaps are bandit and contextual-bandit allocation (Sections 2.9 and 16.7).
key_findings: Section 2.3 (pp. 28-30): On the 10-armed testbed (2000 random bandit problems, 1000 steps, 2000 runs), the greedy method reaches about 1 reward per step against a best possible of about 1.54, and performs significantly worse in the long run because it gets stuck on suboptimal actions.
Section 11.3 (p. 264): The deadly triad of function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy training, combined, can cause instability and divergence in the prediction case.

Section 16.1 (pp. 421-429): TD-Gammon combined TD(lambda) with a multilayer neural network trained on self-play. TD-Gammon 0.0 with essentially zero backgammon knowledge learned to play approximately as well as the best previous backgammon computer after about 300,000 self-play games.
Section 16.1: Adding specialized backgammon features while keeping self-play TD learning produced TD-Gammon 1.0, described as clearly substantially better than all previous backgammon programs.
Section 16.1: The backgammon game tree has an effective branching factor of about 400, too large for conventional heuristic search methods used in chess and checkers.

Section 16.3 (pp. 429-432): Watson Daily-Double wagering used a TD-Gammon-style value function learned over millions of simulated games and chose the bet with the maximum action value. The cited authors report its effectiveness went well beyond what human players do in live play.

Section 16.4 (pp. 429-432): A reinforcement learning memory controller improved on the FR-FCFS controller by 7 percent to 33 percent across nine applications, averaging 19 percent, and closed 27 percent of the gap to an unrealizable Optimistic controller, per the text.

Section 16.6.2 (p. 447): AlphaGo Zero trained over 4.9 million self-play games in about 3 days. In a 100-game match it defeated the AlphaGo version that beat Lee Sedol in all 100 games. Reported Elo ratings: 4308 for AlphaGo Zero, 3739 for the Lee Sedol version, 3144 for the Fan Hui version.
Section 16.7 (p. 450): Personalized delivery of news or advertisements is framed as a contextual bandit problem, because a non-associative bandit does not personalize content delivery.
Chapter 1 (pp. 8-13): The tic-tac-toe example learns position value estimates from self-play using a temporal-difference style update; this is the book framing example for the core RL idea.
extraction.limitations: Preface: the book is an introduction and makes no attempt at comprehensive coverage of a field that has exploded in many directions. Chapter 16 includes only a handful of applications, out of necessity.

summary_md: Sutton and Barto's second edition is the standard textbook on reinforcement learning (RL): an agent learns a policy by trial and error so as to maximize cumulative reward. It moves from k-armed bandits and the exploration-exploitation trade-off (Ch. 2), through finite MDPs, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo and temporal-difference learning (Ch. 3-7), to model-based planning (Ch. 8), function approximation and the deadly triad (Ch. 9-11), eligibility traces, policy gradients, psychology and neuroscience, and case studies (Ch. 16). It contains no social-science data. Its evidence is simulation (on the 10-armed testbed, greedy averages about 1 reward per step against a best of about 1.54) plus reported applications: TD-Gammon after about 300,000 self-play games, AlphaGo Zero after 4.9 million self-play games, and Adobe ad policies scored by high-confidence off-policy evaluation on bank-website logs. For Paul's systems the book is mainly vocabulary and foundation, not evidence. It underlies the RL influence-maximization papers in the vault (Chen 2021 and 2023, RELINK) that Paul maps to the seed gate and the allocator. Measured against the code, the joint CU optimizer is a one-shot, model-based plan. It runs greedy against modeled flip probabilities, never explores, and ingests no observed outcomes (observations=[]). It replans only after modeled threshold crossings. In the book's terms it is pure exploitation of a fixed model, with a myopic single-period objective. The book also sharpens a feasibility limit on Paul's expectation that a learned policy will replace greedy. Its successes needed hundreds of thousands to millions of episodes, but a real CU allocation gives roughly one episode per two-year cycle. Any learned policy would therefore be trained inside the same unvalidated simulator. Section 16.7 points to the more transferable idea: evaluate a candidate allocation policy off-policy from logged contacts and funding, with propensities. The prospective contract does not do this.

bearings.paper_claim: Acting greedily on current value estimates without exploration can lock onto suboptimal actions. On the 10-armed testbed (2000 independent problems, 1000 steps each), the greedy method averages about 1 reward per step against a best possible of about 1.54, and epsilon-greedy does better in the long run. Planning on an incorrect model is likely to compute a suboptimal policy (Sec. 8.3); planning uses a model, learning from experience uses observed interactions (Sec. 8.1).
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 2.2-2.3, pp. 27-30; Sec. 8.1, pp. 159-161; Sec. 8.3 (When the Model Is Wrong)
bearings.system_side: fec/engine/optimize.py allocates a CU budget (default $2.5M in $500 increments, with a per-member cap PMAX) by lazy greedy on modeled marginals of flip_value. The loop stops at the budget or when no positive marginal remains, so spend can fall short of the pot. It has no exploration term. observations is an empty list reserved for real outcomes. It replans after a modeled defection threshold is crossed (the conversions list), so it is not a one-shot plan. In RL terms it is greedy exploitation of a modeled response with no feedback from observed outcomes.

gaps_exposed: No component learns from observed outcomes. The optimizer, budget frontier and per-topic allocators all exploit fixed modeled response curves, and none has an exploration or feedback loop. The observations field in optimize.py is reserved but always empty.

The seed gate implements Chen 2021's contingency concept as a hand-set SGATE table (moneyball_core.py:626-630). None of the RL machinery that Paul's cited sources build on (Q-learning, policy learning) is present, and nothing estimates SGATE values from data.

There is no logged-policy record (who was contacted or funded, when, and with what propensity), so the off-policy evaluation of alternative allocation policies described in Sec. 16.7 is not possible yet.

The allocation objective is single-cycle. Effects that carry across cycles from repeated giving are not modeled, so a myopic-versus-long-horizon comparison (the CTR-versus-LTV contrast) cannot be run.
